title: Filter-Enhanced Smartphone Hyperspectral Imaging
claim: Adding filtered auxiliary camera images to a multi-input reconstruction network yields more accurate outputs than a single-image baseline.
layout: 3 zones, left-to-right, two stacked rows (baseline vs ours), spectra plots at right
description: The figure has two stacked rows that compare a baseline with the proposed system. The top row shows a smartphone with a single raw photo, a plus sign, and a grey 'HSR' neural network. An arrow leads to a hyperspectral cube, with PSNR 31.55, SAM 5.18 and NSE 11.71. The bottom row shows a smartphone whose auxiliary cameras carry red and blue 'SPECTRAL FILTERS'. It takes three raw photos (one plain, one reddish, one bluish), then a plus sign and a green 'MI-HSR' network. An arrow leads to a second cube, with better metrics: PSNR 34.47, SAM 3.85 and NSE 8.45. Yellow points marked on the cubes link by vertical lines to two spectral plots on the right. In those plots, radiance is plotted against wavelength for Point 1 and Point 2. The ground truth (black), the one-input estimate (dashed grey) and the three-input estimate (green) are compared. The green curve tracks the ground truth more closely. Green marks the proposed method and grey marks the baseline.
caption: Proposed low-cost mobile spectral imaging system that transforms a standard smartphone into a spectrally diverse capture device via external filters on auxiliary cameras. This configuration enables multi-channel acquisition without internal hardware modification, supporting practical and scalable hyperspectral reconstruction.
abstract: Hyperspectral reconstruction from RGB imagery offers an affordable alternative to costly hyperspectral acquisition devices. However, its accuracy is fundamentally constrained by the limited spectral resolution of standard RGB cameras. In this paper, we propose a new approach that leverages the multi-camera systems integrated into most modern smartphones and enhances their capabilities by modulating their spectral response functions using carefully selected spectral filters, enabling a smartphone to capture richer spectral information. We propose a neural network able to exploit auxiliary RGB images with diverse spectral characteristics, enabling more accurate hyperspectral reconstruction compared to conventional single-image methods. Training is supported by a newly collected dataset, Doomer, which consists of multiple misaligned RGB images alongside corresponding hyperspectral data. We also propose a device-adaptation strategy that conditions the multi-image hyperspectral reconstruction network on camera color correction matrices available in standard DNG metadata, requiring no real images from the target device. We evaluate it on three physical smartphones, two of them unseen during training.
